one_liner: Haxe's typed-bytecode VM with an x86-64 JIT and a C backend (HL/C); several times faster than the older NekoVM target.
what_it_does: HashLink runs Haxe programs compiled with 'haxe -hl out.hl' either on the hl executable (bytecode loaded and JIT-compiled at startup) or, with 'haxe -hl out.c', as generated C that you build against libhl with your own C compiler (HL/C). It replaces Neko as Haxe's VM target and ships native extension libraries (.hdll) for SDL, OpenAL, image formats, SSL, libuv and SQLite used by the Heaps game engine. It is not a drop-in for Neko: you switch the Haxe target, and Neko-specific APIs and .ndll extensions do not carry over.
how_it_is_fast: Haxe's static types are kept in a strictly typed, register-based bytecode, so the JIT (one 4,771-line jit.c in 1.16) can emit x86/x86-64 machine code with integer registers and SSE scalar float instructions (ADDSD, MULSD) from each function's typed opcodes. HL/C goes further by handing the same typed code to an optimizing C compiler (gcc -O3 in the repo's bench script). Memory is managed by a non-moving, mostly precise mark collector over 64 KB pages, with parallel mark threads (up to 16 on master; 'multiple mark threads' since 1.14).
when_to_use: Haxe projects still on the Neko target (tools, servers, scripts): in a third-party run HL JIT finished the repo's 7-program suite in 5.65 s vs Neko 27.12 s (about 4.8x, 12.8x without Mandelbrot), and 2.00 s vs 21.62 s (about 10.8x) in the 2025 rerun (derived from page data)
Games and desktop apps built with Heaps on x86-64 Windows, Linux or macOS, where the JIT gives fast edit-run cycles and HL/C gives a native release build
When you want hot reload, the HashLink CPU profiler or the VS Code debugger during development, then ship HL/C
Consoles and ARM targets via HL/C, since the generated C only needs libhl and a C11 compiler
when_not_to_use: Raw throughput on allocation-heavy code: in the same 2018 table HL took 4.28 s on Mandelbrot (allocates a Complex object per iteration) vs 0.13 s for hxcpp and 0.10 s for Node, and 1.32 s vs 0.07 s (Node and JVM) in 2025; hxcpp, JVM and JS targets are faster across the suite
ARM64 with the JIT: the 1.16 JIT errors out on ARM ('only x86 and x86-64 are supported, please use HashLink/C') and the Makefile skips building the hl VM on arm64; only HL/C works there
Non-Haxe languages: the bytecode is produced only by the Haxe compiler, so this is not a general embeddable VM like the catalogued Wasm runtimes

Tracking master in production: master is HL_VERSION 2.0 with a restructured JIT (jit_emit.c, jit_regs.c, jit_x86_64.c) and an open regression (#988, 'JIT ERROR get_tmp_args:294 (Too many arguments)', not seen on the 1.16 tag); use the 1.16 release
Latency-sensitive apps with large heaps: the GC is non-generational stop-the-world marking (threads are paused via gc_stop_world), so pause time grows with live heap size

integration.dependencies: core libhl: libc, libm, pthread, bundled PCRE2; optional .hdll libraries: libpng, libturbojpeg, libvorbis (fmt), OpenAL, SDL3 plus GLU (sdl), mbedTLS (ssl), libuv, SQLite, MySQL; the Haxe compiler to produce .hl or HL/C output
integration.min_toolchain: C11 compiler (Makefile uses -std=c11 -O3); Visual Studio solution hl.sln on Windows; SDL3 must be built from source on current Ubuntu per the README
integration.platforms: JIT (hl): x86 and x86-64 on Windows, Linux, macOS; HL/C: any platform with a C11 compiler, including arm64 (the Makefile builds only libhl and .hdll files on arm64)
integration.thread_safety: Multithreaded builds (HL_THREADS) are supported; the GC pauses registered threads for marking (gc_stop_world), so native threads that touch HL values must be registered (hl_register_thread); thread safety of Haxe-level data structures is not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same Haxe source recompiled with -hl instead of -neko, but Neko-specific packages and .ndll native extensions do not carry over

gotchas: Harness resolution: the bench script subtracts a startup estimate (the _Startup.hx run) and truncates each time to 10 ms (Std.int(et*100)/100), and five of seven HL cells are 0.03-0.13 s, so per-test ratios such as FloatArray 48x are resolution-limited; Mandelbrot alone is 76% of HL's 2018 total. When a single benchmark is selected, _Startup is skipped and the reported time is not startup-corrected.

No usable HL/C numbers in the 2025 rerun: every hlc cell is 'hlc result 0 but expected N', and 0 is the _Startup program's expected result, so each benchmark ran a stale _Startup hlc binary (or stale generated C) rather than failing; the hl JIT column is unaffected.

Evidence is a personal gist with a modified script (it adds cs, java, lua, php and python targets that Benchs.hx does not have) and no Haxe, HashLink or Neko versions; the 'lua' and 'python' columns are Haxe compiled to those targets, not stock Lua or CPython, and Neko is HashLink's own predecessor, a weak baseline.

HL JIT is much slower than HL/C or native C on numeric code: haddock7/hashlink_benchmark (OpenSimplex noise, HashLink 1.11.0, i7-7500U) has HL VM 16.76 s, HL/C 5.91 s, native C 3.88 s (HL VM 4.32x slower than native).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling runs Haxe: pick HashLink when your code is Haxe and you are moving off Neko, or want JIT development plus an HL/C release build; for a general-purpose embeddable bytecode VM for other languages, pick a Wasm runtime such as WAMR or wasm3 instead.
verified_claims_summary: A third-party gist ran the repo's other/benchs suite (7 Haxe programs, each run as a process for at least 1 s, startup subtracted) on an Intel Core i5-6600 under Arch Linux in 2018: HashLink JIT took 5.65 s in total vs NekoVM 27.12 s (about 4.8x), and the author's 2025 rerun on a Ryzen 7 7700 gives 2.00 s vs 21.62 s (about 10.8x); versions are not stated and HashLink loses to the hxcpp, JVM and Node targets in both runs (ratios derived from page data).
status_note: Actively maintained by the Haxe Foundation (commits to 2026-10-06, release 1.16 plus nightlies; master is 2.0 development with a reworked JIT), MIT-licensed and copyable, but only useful to Haxe code and its JIT is x86/x86-64 only.
